history.heading: Funan and the Khmer Empire
paragraphs: The earliest known state in the region, Funan, flourished from the 1st century CE as a trading centre influenced by Indian culture. It was followed by Chenla. In 802 Jayavarman II founded the Khmer Empire, which became the dominant power in mainland Southeast Asia.

The empire built Angkor, one of the largest urban complexes of the pre-industrial world, with an advanced water management system. Angkor Wat, built in the 12th century under Suryavarman II as a Hindu temple and later used for Buddhist worship, is the largest religious monument in the world. Jayavarman VII built Angkor Thom and the Bayon temple.

history.heading: Decline and French protectorate
paragraphs: After the 15th century the capital moved south, toward Phnom Penh, and Cambodia was squeezed between the expanding Thai and Vietnamese states, losing territory and influence. In 1863 King Norodom accepted a French protectorate, and Cambodia became part of French Indochina.

history.heading: Independence, war and the Khmer Rouge
paragraphs: Cambodia gained independence in 1953 under King Norodom Sihanouk, who tried to keep the country neutral during the Vietnam War. He was overthrown in 1970, and the country was drawn into the war, suffering heavy US bombing.

In 1975 the communist Khmer Rouge, led by Pol Pot, took power. They emptied the cities and forced people into rural labour camps. Through executions, starvation, overwork and disease, around 1.5 to 2 million people, perhaps a quarter of the population, died. Vietnam invaded in 1979 and ousted the Khmer Rouge.

history.heading: Rebuilding
paragraphs: Civil war continued through the 1980s. The 1991 Paris Peace Accords led to UN-run elections in 1993 and the restoration of the monarchy. Hun Sen, prime minister from 1985, dominated politics for nearly four decades; his son Hun Manet succeeded him in 2023. A UN-backed tribunal convicted senior Khmer Rouge leaders of crimes including genocide.
In 2025 a border dispute with Thailand escalated into deadly clashes before a ceasefire.

culture.heading: Language and religion
paragraphs: Khmer is the national language, with its own script. Theravada Buddhism is the state religion and shapes daily life; most young men traditionally spend time as monks. There are Cham Muslim, Vietnamese and Chinese minorities.
Khmer New Year in April and Pchum Ben, a festival honouring ancestors, are major celebrations.

culture.heading: Arts
paragraphs: Khmer classical dance, the Royal Ballet of Cambodia, with its graceful gestures, is recognised by UNESCO, as is Sbek Thom shadow theatre. The arts were nearly wiped out under the Khmer Rouge, when many artists were killed, and have been revived since.
Cambodian food includes fish amok (a fish curry steamed in banana leaves), prahok (fermented fish paste) and kuy teav noodle soup.

politics.heading: Dominant-party state
paragraphs: Cambodia is formally a constitutional monarchy and multiparty democracy, with King Norodom Sihamoni as head of state. In practice, the Cambodian People's Party has dominated, and the main opposition party was dissolved by court order in 2017; critics describe the system as authoritarian.
Cambodia has close ties with China, a major investor and lender, and is a member of ASEAN.

economy.heading: Rapid growth
paragraphs: Cambodia's economy grew rapidly from the late 1990s. Garment, footwear and travel goods manufacturing is the largest export sector, and tourism, centred on Angkor, is a major source of income. Agriculture, especially rice, remains important.

Construction and real estate have boomed, largely with Chinese investment. The US dollar is widely used alongside the riel. Online scam compounds run by criminal networks have become a serious problem in the region.
